claims.text: The low-field magnetocaloric response and hysteresis of as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type nanoribbons are jointly governed by confinement-related strain effects and extrinsic heat-transfer limitations.
Nanoribbons with nanoscale widths inherently exhibit lateral strain gradients.
An approximately 10 nm Cu or diamond-like-carbon interfacial layer can serve as a high-thermal-conductivity heat sink beneath the nanoribbons.
The interfacial heat-sink layer reduces transient thermal gradients at the HEA–substrate interface.
Lateral strain gradients affect magnetic domain configurations in the nanoribbons.
Lateral confinement-induced strain gradients modify local magnetic anisotropy.
Lateral confinement-induced strain gradients modify domain-wall behavior.
Strain-mediated changes in anisotropy and domain-wall behavior shift the magnetocaloric entropy-change peak.
Strain-mediated changes in anisotropy and domain-wall behavior broaden the magnetocaloric entropy-change peak.
Strain-mediated changes in domain-wall behavior enhance hysteresis.
Limited heat transfer in the as-deposited structures produces a lag between thermal response and the applied magnetic field.
Thermal lag broadens the magnetocaloric response.
Thermal lag increases hysteretic losses.
Improved interfacial heat dissipation reduces thermal lag.
Heat-sink-supported nanoribbons will exhibit a sharper magnetocaloric entropy-change peak than otherwise identical baseline nanoribbons.
Heat-sink-supported nanoribbons will exhibit lower hysteresis losses than otherwise identical baseline nanoribbons.
The effects of the heat-sink layer will become more pronounced at higher magnetic-cooling cycle frequencies.
The proposed operating boundaries are ribbon widths of approximately 100–500 nm, applied fields below 200 Oe, and temperatures of 100–300 K.
Annealing, recrystallization, and large-scale structural transformations are negligible in the as-deposited samples under the stated conditions.
Failure to observe peak sharpening, hysteresis reduction, and a significant decrease in thermal lag relative to the no-heat-sink control would falsify the proposed heat-transfer mechanism.
